reels.title: Why data tools act strangely

beats.say: Why does your data tool sometimes show an old number, or the same order twice?
Picture a pizza chain with ten shops sharing one order book. Each shop keeps its own copy, because one copy would die if that shop burned down.
The phone lines between shops are slow and sometimes drop. So one shop may read an out of date copy. Or a call gets repeated, and an order is made twice.

Every data tool is those shops. Kafka, Spark and Snowflake all copy and split data across many machines. Learn the rules of the shops, and the odd behavior stops being a mystery. It also lets you explain why, in an interview.

check.q: A shop reads an out of date order book. What is the best explanation?
opts: The copy had not yet received the latest update
The data was deleted forever
The shop has no copy at all
check.why: Copies are updated over slow, unreliable links, so a replica can briefly lag behind the newest write.

work: List the tools you run and note which ones keep several copies of data.
Recall one past incident with stale or duplicate data and guess which copy lagged or which message repeated.

reels.title: Copy and split: how tools stay alive

beats.say: Kafka keeps three copies of each partition. One broker dies at noon. Why is nothing lost?
Each partition has one leader and two followers. Producers write to the leader. Followers copy the log, and the leader waits for them before saying done.
When the leader dies, a follower that is caught up becomes the new leader. The data was already on it. The same idea, copy first then acknowledge, shows up in Postgres replication too.

The other half is splitting. Kafka puts events with the same key, like trip id, in one partition, so their order is kept. Spark cuts a table into, say, two hundred partitions so many machines work at once.

check.q: Why key Kafka events by trip_id?
opts: It makes the topic smaller
Events with the same key land in one partition, so their order is preserved
It removes the need for replication
check.why: Kafka orders only within a partition, and the key decides the partition, so one trip's events stay in sequence.

work: Check the replication factor and minimum in-sync replicas on your most important topic.
Look at the partition key for one pipeline and ask whether it keeps related events together.

reels.title: Duplicates, stale reads, lost updates

beats.say: Your producer timed out, retried, and now every event appears twice. Whose fault is that?
Nobody's. A timeout cannot tell a lost request from a lost reply. So the sender retries, and the receiver may have already stored the first one. That gives at least once delivery.
The fix is idempotence: give each message an id, so a repeat is ignored. Same story for stale reads. A replica lags the leader by a few seconds, so a read right after a write can miss it.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Message id makes a repeat harmless
Read from the leader after a write

beats.say: Lost updates come from two writers reading the same value. Iceberg handles it with optimistic concurrency: commit only if nobody changed the table, otherwise retry.

check.q: A retried write created duplicates. What is the most robust fix?
opts: Disable all retries
Make the write idempotent with a unique message id
Add more replicas
check.why: Retries are needed because timeouts are ambiguous. Idempotent writes make repeats harmless instead of risking data loss.

work: Find one pipeline sink and confirm it dedupes by a stable id or uses upserts.
Test a read right after a write on a replica and measure the lag.
Review how concurrent writers to one Iceberg table handle commit conflicts.

reels.title: Choosing the guarantee you pay for

beats.say: Why not make every system strongly consistent and stop worrying?
Because agreement costs round trips. Waiting for a majority across regions can add a hundred milliseconds to every write. And during a network split the minority side must refuse requests.

So match the guarantee to the need. Payments and inventory counts need it. A clickstream dashboard does not. At least once plus dedupe is far cheaper. An LSM store suits write heavy loads, because it appends sequentially, but reads and compaction cost more.

show.title: Match guarantee to need
items: Clickstream: at least once plus dedupe

beats.say: In an interview, name the trade. Say what you give up, what it costs, and what you would pick instead if the workload flips.

check.q: A dashboard counts page views and tolerates small delays. Which design fits best?
opts: Cross-region strongly consistent writes
At least once delivery with dedupe and eventual consistency
A single machine with no replication
check.why: The workload tolerates staleness, so paying latency and availability costs for strong consistency is wasteful. Dedupe handles repeats cheaply.

work: For each of your key datasets, write down the consistency it truly needs.
In your next design review, state one trade-off and the alternative you rejected.

reels.title: Three ways to organize a filing room

beats.say: Why is one database fast at saving data, and another fast at answering huge questions?

show.sub: The layout decides what is fast.

beats.say: Think of a library. A B-tree is the card catalog. Every book has a fixed shelf spot, so you find any book in a few steps. But adding a book means fitting it into its exact place.

chip.text: Fast to find, fiddly to insert

beats.say: An LSM-tree is an inbox tray. New notes just drop on top, instantly. Later, a clerk sorts the pile into neat stacks. Saving is fast, but finding a note may mean checking several stacks.
A column store keeps all the ages in one drawer, all the cities in another. To average ages, you open one drawer instead of every customer folder.

check.q: Which layout suits averaging one field across millions of customers?
opts: Card catalog (B-tree)
Inbox tray (LSM-tree)
Drawers per field (column store)
check.why: A column store opens only the drawer for that one field, so it reads far less data than layouts that keep whole rows together.

work: Name one table you own and say whether it is mostly looked up, mostly written, or mostly summed.
Explain the library analogy to a teammate in under a minute.

reels.title: Why B-trees find a row in four reads

beats.say: How can a database find one row among a billion in just four page reads?
The table is split into pages, eight kilobytes in Postgres. A B plus tree node is one page holding hundreds of keys. With hundreds of branches per level, three or four levels cover a billion rows.
The top levels are small, so they stay in memory. Only the last one or two reads touch disk. Disk reads are the slow part, so fewer pages means a faster query.

chip.text: Cost is roughly pages from disk

beats.say: Values sit only in the leaves, and the leaves are linked. For a range, descend once, then walk sideways along the leaves.

show.title: Range scans
items: Descend once to the first key
No need to climb back up

check.q: Why does a B+tree over a billion rows need only about four levels?
opts: Each node is a page holding hundreds of keys
Rows are stored in memory
It keeps only one key per node
check.why: Hundreds of branches per page means the fan-out multiplies quickly, so very few levels cover a huge table.

work: Look up your database's page size and estimate the index depth of your biggest table.
Check that range queries on your key use the leaf order, such as a date range on an indexed date.

reels.title: How an LSM-tree writes so fast

beats.say: How can a database accept hundreds of thousands of writes a second without slowing down?
An LSM-tree never edits data in place. Each write is appended to a log for safety, and put in a sorted memory table called the memtable. Both are sequential, which disks love.
When the memtable fills, it is flushed as one sorted, immutable file, an SSTable. Files pile up.
A read checks the memtable, then newest files first. Bloom filters, small summaries, skip files that cannot hold the key. Compaction merges files, keeps the newest value, and drops deleted data.

check.q: What does a bloom filter do on an LSM read?
opts: Merges files
Skips files that cannot contain the key
Compresses the memtable
check.why: It is a compact summary that says definitely not here or maybe here, so the read avoids useless file lookups.

work: Find out how many SSTables a typical read touches in your LSM store.
Watch compaction throughput during peak writes.

reels.title: Why the planner ignores your index

beats.say: Why does the same query use an index on Monday and ignore it on Tuesday?

The planner estimates how many rows match, using table statistics. Few rows: index scan, jumping to each row. A moderate number: bitmap scan, which collects the pages first and reads each once in disk order.
If most of the table matches, a sequential scan wins, because reading pages in order beats thousands of random jumps. If the index holds every needed column, an index-only scan skips the table.

show.title: Why plans flip
items: Many matches: random jumps cost more than one sweep
Covering index: answer comes from the index alone

beats.say: Run explain analyze. A big gap between estimated and actual rows means stale statistics, or a predicate like a function on the column.

show.title: Check the estimate
show.text:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;
-- compare estimated rows vs actual rows

check.q: Estimated rows are 10 but actual rows are 2 million. Likely cause?
opts: The disk is full
Stale statistics or an unusable predicate
The index is too small
check.why: A huge gap means the planner chose from wrong information, often outdated statistics or a function on the column hiding the index.

work: Run explain analyze on your slowest query and compare estimated and actual rows.
Refresh statistics on tables that changed a lot.

reels.title: Surviving a crash, and the UUID trap

beats.say: If the power dies mid-write, how does a database not lose your committed data?
A change goes to the page in memory and to an append-only write-ahead log. The log is flushed to disk before commit returns. Dirty pages can be written later.
After a crash, the database replays the log to rebuild what was lost. Checkpoints write dirty pages in the background, so old log can be recycled.
Key choice matters too. Random UUID primary keys scatter inserts across leaves and cause page splits. Time-ordered ids, like bigint or UUID version seven, append at the right edge.

check.q: Why is the log flushed before COMMIT returns?
opts: So pages never need writing
So a crash can be replayed without losing committed changes
So reads are faster
check.why: Once the log is on disk, the change survives a crash even if the data pages were never written.

work: Review primary key types on large tables and consider time-ordered ids.
Check the fsync and commit settings for your durability needs.

reels.title: Tombstones and amplification

beats.say: Why can an LSM database get slower after you delete a lot of data?
A delete cannot edit an immutable file. It writes a tombstone, a marker saying this key is gone. Reads must scan past tombstones until compaction finally removes them.
Compaction rewrites files, so one logical write may be physically written many times. That is write amplification. It also burns I/O and CPU.
Reads suffer read amplification: one lookup may touch several files. Bloom filters help point lookups, but not much for range scans.

show.title: Read side
items: One read may touch many files

check.q: After mass deletes in an LSM store, reads slow down because:
opts: Tombstones must be scanned past until compaction
Memory is erased
Bloom filters stop working entirely
check.why: Deleted data remains in files alongside tombstones until compaction purges both, so reads wade through them.

work: Avoid delete-heavy queue patterns on LSM stores.
Monitor tombstone counts and compaction backlog.

reels.title: Choosing B-tree, LSM or columns

beats.say: You are picking storage for three workloads. How do you choose between B-tree, LSM and columns?
A transactional app with many reads and updates: B-tree, like Postgres. Predictable reads, but random writes and page splits cost you.

show.title: B-tree
items: Fast point reads and range scans

beats.say: Event ingestion or time series at huge write rates: LSM, like Cassandra or RocksDB. You pay with compaction cost and read amplification.
Analytics scanning a few columns of billions of rows: columnar, like Parquet. Compression and min max statistics skip data. Never run select star there.

show.title: Columnar
items: Min and max stats skip blocks

beats.say: Every secondary index adds write cost and space. Lakehouses use partition pruning, statistics, clustering and bloom filters instead.

show.sub: each one is updated on every write

check.q: A sensor platform ingests 500,000 events per second with simple key lookups. Best fit?
opts: B-tree OLTP database
LSM-tree store
Columnar warehouse as the primary write path
check.why: Sequential appends give LSM very high write throughput, and key lookups suit it well, while the compaction cost is acceptable.

work: List your workloads and label each read-heavy, write-heavy or scan-heavy.
Audit secondary indexes and drop those no query uses.
Prefer clustering and partitioning over indexes on lakehouse tables.

reels.title: The filing room that got too full

beats.say: What do you do when one filing cabinet is too full for a single clerk to handle?
You split the files across many cabinets, each with its own clerk. That is partitioning: splitting data so each machine holds only a part. Work now happens in parallel.
But how you split matters. Sort by the first letter of the surname, and the clerk for S is swamped while the clerk for X sits idle. That swamped clerk is a hot spot.
Hand files out by a scrambled number instead, and the load evens out. The cost: finding every surname from A to C now means asking every clerk.

show.title: Scrambling trades one thing for another
items: Looking up one file stays easy
Ranges like A to C need every clerk

check.q: Why does scrambling files across clerks make a range lookup like A to C slower?
opts: Each clerk works more slowly
Neighbouring names end up scattered, so every clerk must be asked
The scramble loses some files
check.why: Scrambling spreads neighbours across all partitions. Even load is gained, but ordered ranges are no longer together.

work: Name one table at work that is mostly written to by a single busy key.
Ask yourself whether your main queries are lookups by id or scans over a range.

reels.title: Range or hash: picking the split

beats.say: Why do today's timestamps crash one server while the other nine nap?

Key range partitioning gives each node a slice, like A to F, or one day of dates. Range scans are fast because neighbours live together. But all new writes carry today's timestamp, so they all hit the newest range.
Hash partitioning runs the key through a hash function and uses the result to pick a node. Ten nodes each get about ten percent of writes. The price: a range query must ask all ten nodes.
So pick by access pattern. Mostly lookups by id? Hash. Mostly range scans over ordered keys? Range, and watch for clustered writes.

check.q: A table is queried mostly by date range, and writes arrive in time order. What is the main risk of range partitioning by timestamp?
opts: Range scans become slow
The newest partition takes all writes
Keys cannot be found
check.why: Range keeps scans efficient, but time-ordered writes all land on the latest range, creating a write hot spot.

work: Check whether any partition key you use is monotonic, like a timestamp or auto-increment id.
Write down the top three queries on a big table before choosing hash or range.

reels.title: Adding a node without moving everything

beats.say: You add one server to a ten-node cluster. How many keys must move?
If you place keys with hash mod N, where N is the node count, going from ten to eleven changes almost every answer. About ninety percent of keys move. That is a huge data shuffle.

show.title: Keys moved when adding an eleventh node

beats.say: Consistent hashing puts nodes and keys on a ring. A key belongs to the next node clockwise. A new node only steals keys from its neighbour, so about one eleventh move.
Nodes can land unevenly on the ring, so each server takes many virtual spots to balance load. Kafka, Elasticsearch and Cassandra go further: fixed partitions, moved whole.

show.title: Keeping rebalancing cheap
items: Virtual nodes even out the ring
Fixed partitions move as whole units
Never use hash mod node count

check.q: Why is hash(key) mod N, with N equal to the node count, a bad placement scheme?
opts: Hashes are not even
Changing N remaps almost every key
It cannot find keys at all
check.why: When N changes, most keys get a different remainder, so nearly all data must move to new nodes.

work: Check how your store rebalances: fixed partitions, a ring, or mod N.
Plan capacity changes in advance so data movement does not happen at peak traffic.

reels.title: Perfect hash, one burning partition

beats.say: Your hash is perfect, yet one partition is on fire. Why?
Hashing spreads different keys evenly. It cannot split one key. A viral post or one giant merchant sends all its traffic to a single partition, however many nodes you own.
Fix one: salting. Add a random suffix, so the key becomes merchant forty-two with a suffix from zero to nine, spreading writes over ten partitions. Reads must now gather all ten and combine them.
Fix two: cache the hot key so reads never reach the partition. Fix three: give it a dedicated partition. Spark skew joins use the same salting trick.

check.q: After salting a hot key into ten sub-keys, what new cost appears?
opts: Writes get slower
Reads must query all sub-keys and combine results
The key can no longer be hashed
check.why: Salting spreads writes, but one logical key now lives in ten places, so a read has to gather and merge them.

work: Find your top ten keys by traffic and see whether one dominates a partition.
Decide per hot key whether caching or salting fits, based on read versus write mix.

reels.title: Kafka: order and parallelism live in partitions

beats.say: Kafka promises ordering, but only in one place. Where?
Order is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across the topic. So key messages by the entity whose order matters, such as trip id or account id. Same key, same partition, same order.
Each partition in a consumer group goes to exactly one consumer. A topic with twelve partitions can keep twelve consumers busy. The thirteenth sits idle.
The partition count is fixed at creation, and raising it later changes which partition a key maps to, breaking per-key order. Plan with headroom.

check.q: A topic has 8 partitions and you run 20 consumers in one group. How many do useful work?
check.why: Each partition goes to exactly one consumer in a group, so at most 8 consumers are active and the rest idle.

work: Check that your Kafka message keys are the entity whose order matters.
Compare each topic's partition count with your peak consumer count.

reels.title: Shard last, not first

beats.say: Should you shard the database? Usually, not yet.

Postgres partitioning splits one table into child tables on the same server, by month or region. Queries skip partitions they do not need, and dropping old data means detaching a partition, instantly, with no slow delete.
Sharding puts rows on different servers. It scales writes, but joins across shards, transactions and resharding all become painful.
So climb the ladder: add indexes, add read replicas, partition the table. Shard only when write volume beats one machine. Then choose a key with even spread that matches your main queries.

check.q: Your single Postgres server is slow on a huge events table, mostly reading recent months. What do you try first?
opts: Shard across many servers
Partition the table by month and add indexes
Rewrite with hash mod N
check.why: Partitioning by month lets queries prune old data cheaply on one server. Sharding adds join, transaction and resharding pain you may not need.

work: Write down the write rate at which one machine genuinely stops being enough.
Before sharding, try partition pruning, indexes and replicas, and measure the gain.

reels.title: Why your update seems to vanish

beats.say: You change your profile photo, refresh the page, and the old photo is back. Did the website lose your change?

show.sub: Did the site lose your change?

beats.say: Not at all. Think of a head office with three branch offices. Head office writes every new price in its master book, then mails copies to the branches. The branches keep working if one office burns down, and customers can ask any branch.
But mail takes time. If you ask a branch before the mail arrives, you get yesterday's price. That delay is called replication lag.
So the photo was never lost. You just asked a branch that had not caught up yet. Copies buy safety and speed, and the price is a short window where they disagree.

show.title: The trade
items: Price: a short window of disagreement

check.q: You update your profile and a refresh shows the old value. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The write was lost forever
The read hit a copy that had not caught up
The database deleted your change
The leader is down
check.why: Replicas receive changes after a delay. Your write is safe on the leader, but the follower you read from lagged behind.

work: Find one screen in your product where users read right after writing.
Ask your team which database node serves that read: leader or replica.

reels.title: Leader, followers, sync and async

beats.say: A leader database just committed your write. Should it wait for followers before saying done?
In single leader replication, every write goes to one leader. It appends the change to its log and streams that log to followers, which replay it in order. Postgres and MySQL work this way.

Synchronous means the leader waits for the follower's acknowledgement. Safe, but if one follower stalls, writes stall too. Asynchronous means it replies immediately. Fast, but if the leader crashes, the last few hundred milliseconds of writes can vanish.
So most systems pick one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous. Kafka does the same with in-sync replicas and acks equals all: a write counts only once every in-sync replica has it.

show.title: The usual compromise
items: Kafka: in-sync replicas plus acks equals all

check.q: Why do many systems use one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous?
opts: It makes followers identical at all times
It guarantees a second durable copy without letting every slow follower block writes
It removes the need for a leader
It lets followers accept writes
check.why: One sync follower means an acknowledged write exists on two machines, while async followers cannot stall the write path.

work: Check your Postgres or MySQL setting for synchronous standbys.
Review Kafka producers: confirm acks equals all and min in-sync replicas is set to at least two.

reels.title: Leaderless quorums: R plus W over N

beats.say: With no leader at all, how can a read still be correct?
In leaderless systems like Cassandra and DynamoDB, the client sends each write to several replicas and reads from several. Say N is three copies. Write to W equals two, read from R equals two.
Two plus two is four, which is more than three. So any read set and write set must share at least one replica, and that one has the newest value. The rule is R plus W greater than N.
Replicas that missed the write get fixed by read repair, where the reader pushes the newest value back, and by background anti-entropy that compares copies.

show.title: How stale copies heal
items: Read repair: reader writes back the newest value

check.q: With N equals 5 and W equals 2, what is the smallest R that guarantees a read overlaps the latest write?
check.why: You need R plus W greater than N, so R plus 2 greater than 5 means R is at least 4. Check: 3 plus 2 equals 5, which is not greater than 5, so 4 is needed.

work: Write down N, W and R for your Cassandra or DynamoDB tables.
Test what a read returns when one replica is down and W equals 1.

reels.title: Lag anomalies interviewers name

beats.say: Why can you see an answer before the question it answers?

show.sub: Lag, not a bug in your code

beats.say: Because followers lag by different amounts. Three anomalies follow. Read-your-writes: you update your profile, then read a lagging follower and see the old value. Fix it by reading your own recent writes from the leader.

chip.text: Fix: read own writes from leader

beats.say: Monotonic reads: two refreshes hit two followers, and the page jumps back in time. Fix it by pinning each user to one replica.

chip.text: Fix: pin user to one replica

beats.say: Consistent prefix: a reply lands on a fast follower before its question lands on a slow one. If the two live in different partitions, nothing orders them. Keep causally related writes in the same partition.

chip.text: Fix: same partition for related writes

check.q: A user refreshes twice and the second page shows older data than the first. Which fix targets this?
opts: Read your own writes from the leader
Pin the user to one replica
Increase the partition count
Switch to asynchronous replication
check.why: Going back in time means the two reads hit followers at different lag. Sticking a user to one replica keeps reads moving forward.

work: Add a short leader-read window after a user writes.
Route sessions by user id hash to a fixed replica.
Key related events, such as question and answer, by the same id.

reels.title: Failover and quorum gotchas

beats.say: The leader just died. Who is in charge now, and what happened to its last writes?

Failover means promoting a follower to leader. With asynchronous replication, the new leader may lack writes the old one acknowledged, so those writes are lost. Worse, if the old leader wakes up still believing it leads, two leaders accept writes. That is split brain.

Quorums have gaps too. A write that reaches only one replica, fewer than W, reports failure but is not rolled back, so a later read may still see it. And with clock-based last write wins, a skewed clock silently drops a newer write.

show.title: Quorum gotchas
items: Failed write below W is not rolled back
Last write wins trusts clocks that can skew
Sloppy quorums can break the overlap guarantee

check.q: Why can failover lose acknowledged writes?
opts: Followers refuse to replay logs
The promoted follower may not yet have writes the old leader acknowledged under async replication
Clients retry too often
Logs are not ordered
check.why: Async replication acknowledges before followers have the write. If the leader dies in that gap, the promoted follower never saw it.

work: Run a failover drill and diff row counts before and after.
Set fencing so an old leader cannot accept writes after demotion.
Avoid last write wins on data where lost updates matter.

reels.title: Choosing a replication model

beats.say: Do you really need multi-region writes, or do you just want them?

Single leader is the default: one order of writes, simple reasoning, and read replicas scale reads cheaply. It scales writes only by partitioning. Choose it unless a leader outage or cross-region write latency is truly unacceptable.

show.title: Default: single leader
items: Move away only if outage or latency forces it

beats.say: Multi-leader and leaderless buy write availability, but you pay with conflicts. Now you need a merge rule, such as last write wins, which loses data, or a conflict-free data type, and every reader must tolerate stale values.

For data pipelines, remember change data capture is replication. Debezium is just a follower reading the Postgres write-ahead log, so watch its lag like any replica's, and never read from it expecting instant truth.

check.q: A team wants multi-leader writes in two regions mainly to cut read latency. What is the better first step?
opts: Adopt multi-leader and use last write wins
Add local read replicas and keep a single write leader
Make all replicas synchronous
Move to leaderless with W equals 1
check.why: Read latency is solved by local read replicas. Multi-leader adds conflict handling you only need when writes themselves must be accepted in several places.

work: List which tables truly need writes in more than one region.
Put lag alerts on read replicas and on CDC connectors.
Document the conflict rule for any multi-writer data before launch.

reels.title: One notebook or many photocopies

beats.say: Why can two phones show you two different answers to the same question? Because there are many copies of the data, and copies take time to match.

show.sub: Many copies take time to match

beats.say: Picture one notebook in an office. Everyone reads and writes the same page. Nobody ever sees old information. That is strong consistency. It is simple, but people queue to use the notebook.

chip.text: Always the latest, but people queue

beats.say: Now give every desk its own photocopy. Work is fast, even if the hallway is blocked. But a copy may be stale for a while. If everyone stops writing, all copies end up the same. That is eventual consistency.
So the choice is: always right but slower, or always quick but sometimes behind.

check.q: In the photocopy picture, what does eventual consistency promise?
opts: Every desk always shows the newest page
If writing stops, all copies end up the same
Copies never differ at any moment
Writes are refused until all copies match
check.why: Eventual consistency only promises convergence once writes stop, with no promise about timing, so stale reads are possible meanwhile.

work: List which of your datasets must never show stale data and which can lag a few seconds.
Next time a dashboard disagrees with a source, check replica lag before suspecting a bug.

reels.title: CAP and PACELC in practice

beats.say: A cable between two data centers is cut. What should the database do?

That cut is a network partition. CAP says you pick one. Stay consistent: the side that cannot reach a majority refuses requests, so it is unavailable. Stay available: both sides keep accepting writes, and they disagree until repaired.

But partitions are rare. Most days the network is fine. PACELC covers that: else, you trade latency for consistency. Waiting for a cross-region replica to confirm might add 80 milliseconds to every write. Skipping the wait is fast, but a reader may see old data.
Most data systems choose available and low latency, then repair the differences later.

check.q: The network is healthy. According to PACELC, what trade-off remains?
opts: Availability against partition tolerance
Latency against consistency
Storage cost against durability
Throughput against schema flexibility
check.why: The else part of PACELC says that with no partition you still trade latency against consistency, for example waiting on remote replicas.

work: For each datastore you run, write down its PACELC leaning: PA/EL or PC/EC.
Measure the latency cost of your strongest consistency setting before you require it.

reels.title: How Raft agrees on one answer

beats.say: Five servers must agree on one answer, and two of them may crash. How?
That is consensus, and Raft does it with majorities. One node is elected leader for a numbered term. Clients send writes only to the leader.

The leader appends the entry to its log and copies it to followers. Once three of the five have it, that is a majority, so the entry is committed and the client gets an answer. Slow followers catch up later.

If the leader dies, followers time out, and one calls an election for term plus one. Any two majorities overlap, so the new leader always has every committed entry. Five nodes survive two failures. You use this in etcd under Kubernetes and Kafka KRaft.

show.title: Failover
items: Timeout, then election for the next term
Used in etcd and Kafka KRaft

check.q: Why can a newly elected Raft leader never lose a committed entry?
opts: It always has the fastest clock
Clients resend every write
Its majority overlaps the majority that committed the entry
It copies the log from the old leader
check.why: Committed means a majority holds the entry, and any new leader needs a majority vote, so at least one voter has the entry.

work: Run consensus clusters with 3 or 5 nodes spread over separate failure zones.
Learn which of your tools hide a Raft or ZooKeeper cluster, and monitor its leader changes.

reels.title: When clocks lie: last write wins

beats.say: Two people update the same record. Why can the later update vanish even though both succeeded?

Because of clocks. Machines drift apart by milliseconds or more, and can jump when they resync. With last write wins, the highest timestamp survives. If server A's clock runs fifty milliseconds fast, its older write beats a genuinely newer one, silently.

Vector clocks avoid trusting time. Each node keeps a counter, and each version carries all the counters. Compare two versions. If one has every counter at least as high, it came after, so keep it. If each is higher somewhere, they are concurrent: a real conflict.
Then you merge or ask the application, instead of losing data quietly.

check.q: Two versions have vector clocks A1 B0 and A0 B1. What does that mean?
opts: The first is older, so discard it
The second is newer by a counter
They are concurrent and conflict
They are identical
check.why: Each version is higher in one counter and lower in another, so neither happened before the other; they are concurrent.

work: Find any last write wins rule in your pipelines and ask what happens if a clock is 100 ms off.
Prefer version numbers or event sequence ids over wall-clock timestamps for ordering.

reels.title: Fencing tokens stop zombie leaders

beats.say: A leader freezes for ten seconds during garbage collection. It wakes up and still thinks it is in charge. What happens to your data?

show.sub: It still thinks it is in charge

beats.say: Its lease expired while it slept, and a new leader took over. But the old one does not know. It sends a write to storage, and overwrites newer work. A check before writing does not help, because the pause can strike right after the check.

The fix is a fencing token. Each lease gets a number that only grows. Leader one gets token thirty-three. The new leader gets thirty-four. Storage remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects anything lower. The stale write with thirty-three bounces.
So safety comes from the storage, not from the leader's belief.

check.q: Why is checking that I still hold the lease right before writing not enough?
opts: Leases never expire
The pause can happen after the check
Storage cannot read leases
Checks are too slow
check.why: A pause or network delay can strike between the check and the write, so only the storage rejecting old tokens is safe.

work: Check whether your lock or lease service hands out a monotonically increasing token.
Make downstream writers reject any token lower than the highest seen.

reels.title: When not to pay for consensus

beats.say: Should every database use consensus and strong consistency? Usually no, and the reason is cost.

show.sub: Usually no. It has a cost.

beats.say: Every committed write waits for a majority round trip. Across regions that is tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and throughput is capped by one leader. Add nodes and writes do not get faster; they can get slower, since more acknowledgments are needed.

So spend consensus where wrongness is expensive: leader election, locks, metadata, money. Keep it small, three or five nodes in one region or close by. For high-volume data like clickstreams, use eventual consistency, idempotent writes and repair.

show.title: Where to spend it
items: Use: leader election, locks, metadata, money
Keep it small: 3 or 5 nodes, close together
Use idempotent writes and repair instead

beats.say: Also avoid even-sized clusters: four nodes tolerate only one failure, the same as three. And never rely on wall clocks for ordering; use logical versions or fencing tokens.

check.q: Which workload is the best fit for a Raft-backed store?
opts: Billions of clickstream events per day
Cluster leader election and config metadata
Cross-region cache of product images
Append-only logs with no readers
check.why: Small, critical, rarely written state where disagreement is costly justifies consensus. High-volume events do not.

work: Audit where you pay for strong consistency and downgrade any path that tolerates stale reads.
Standardize on odd cluster sizes, and keep consensus clusters small and in one region.

reels.title: The cheque you mailed twice

beats.say: You mail a cheque and hear nothing back. Do you send another?

show.sub: A missing reply could mean lost, late or delivered

beats.say: That is the whole problem. The post office can lose letters, delay them, or deliver twice. You cannot tell which happened, because silence looks the same every time.
So you pick a rule. Send once and forget, and letters can vanish. Resend until a receipt arrives, and the bank may get two cheques.
The fix is to number every cheque. The bank sees number forty-two twice and ignores the copy. Resending becomes safe. That is exactly once in effect.

check.q: A sender retries a message because no reply came. What makes the retry safe?
opts: Sending it only once
Each message has a number so the receiver ignores copies
Waiting a long time before retrying
check.why: Retries guarantee delivery but can duplicate. A unique number lets the receiver drop duplicates, so the effect happens once.

work: List where your pipelines retry and ask what happens when a retry duplicates a record.
Find one place where a unique id could make a repeat harmless.

reels.title: How Kafka drops retried duplicates

beats.say: A Kafka producer sends a record, the network hiccups, and no acknowledgement comes back. Did the broker store it?
The producer cannot know, so it retries. Without protection, the broker writes the record twice, and your count is off by one.
Idempotent mode fixes this. Each producer gets an id, and every record carries a sequence number. The broker remembers the last number per partition.
When the retry arrives with sequence seven again, the broker sees it already has seven, drops the copy, and still acknowledges. Retries now cost nothing.

check.q: How does the broker recognise a retried record under the idempotent producer?
opts: It compares the record bytes with every stored record
It sees a producer id and sequence number it already stored
It waits for the consumer to complain
check.why: The broker tracks the last sequence per producer id and partition, so a repeated pair is dropped cheaply.

work: Turn on the idempotent producer setting and keep retries enabled.
Test it by killing the network mid-send and counting records on the topic.

reels.title: Checkpoints, replay and safe sinks

beats.say: A Flink job crashes at three in the morning. How does it resume without losing or double counting anything?
Every few seconds it takes a checkpoint: a consistent snapshot of its running state plus the exact source offsets it has read up to.
After a crash, it restores the last snapshot and rewinds the source to those offsets. Everything after the snapshot gets replayed, so the sink may see some records twice.
That is fine if the sink is idempotent. Merge on a key, overwrite a partition, or commit atomically to an Iceberg table. The replay lands on the same result.

show.title: Sinks that absorb replay
items: Atomic table commit, as in Iceberg

check.q: After a checkpoint restore, some output is written twice. What keeps the final result correct?
opts: A larger checkpoint interval
An idempotent or transactional sink
Restarting the job from offset zero
check.why: Replay is at least once. The sink must make repeated writes harmless, for example by merging on a key.

work: Check each sink: is it a keyed merge, a partition overwrite or a transactional commit?
Kill a job on purpose and confirm the output has no duplicates.

reels.title: Event time and the watermark

beats.say: A phone records a tap at noon, goes through a tunnel, and uploads at twelve fifteen. Which time counts?
Event time is when it happened. Processing time is when your system saw it. Counting by processing time puts the tap in the wrong window, and results change on every replay.
So windows use event time. But then, when is the noon window done? Late events may still be coming.
A watermark is the system's guess: no events older than this will arrive. Set it five minutes behind the newest event, and the window closes then. Later arrivals are dropped or routed aside.

show.title: Watermark rules
items: Watermark = newest event time minus 5 minutes
Window closes when the watermark passes its end
Too-late events: drop or side output
Bigger delay: more accurate, slower results

check.q: What does a watermark of newest event time minus five minutes mean?
opts: Events up to five minutes late are still counted; older ones are treated as late
Every event is delayed exactly five minutes
The job checkpoints every five minutes
check.why: The watermark estimates completeness. Windows close when it passes their end, so only events later than the allowed delay are late.

work: Measure how late your real events arrive, then set the watermark delay from that data.
Route too-late events to a side output so you can count what you drop.

reels.title: Why exactly once still sends two emails

beats.say: Your pipeline claims exactly once, yet customers got two emails. How?
Checkpoints only protect state inside the engine. An email, an API call or a write to a plain database happens outside it, and replay fires it again.
Replay also needs deterministic code. If you use random numbers or the current clock, the second run produces different output, so duplicates are not identical and a key cannot catch them.

show.title: Replay must repeat itself
items: Avoid random values and the current clock
Derive ids from the data, not the run

beats.say: With Kafka transactions, a stuck old producer, called a zombie, may wake up and write. Fencing by epoch rejects it. And consumers must read committed only, or they see aborted data.

show.title: Transaction gotchas
items: Zombie producer wakes after a pause

check.q: A replayed job calls a payment API directly and charges twice. What is the best fix?
opts: Increase the checkpoint frequency
Send an idempotency key derived from the event with each call
Switch the job to at most once
check.why: External effects are outside the checkpoint. A deterministic key lets the receiver ignore the repeated call.

work: List every external side effect in your jobs and attach a stable idempotency key.
Search for random or current-time calls in code that can be replayed.

reels.title: When not to pay for exactly once

beats.say: Should every pipeline be exactly once? Usually not, and chasing it can cost you.
Transactions and checkpoints add latency: output waits for commit, so a one second checkpoint means results appear a second or more later. They also add state storage and operational complexity.
If the sink is naturally keyed, at least once plus upsert gives the same correctness for far less. For metrics where one percent error is fine, at most once may be enough.

show.title: Cheaper choices
items: Keyed sink: at least once plus upsert

beats.say: Choose by cost of a duplicate versus cost of delay. Money movement: idempotency keys and transactional commits. Dashboards: keep it simple. And say it plainly: exactly once delivery does not exist.

show.title: Say it in the interview
items: Money: idempotency keys plus transactional commits
Exactly once delivery does not exist
Exactly once effect = at least once + idempotent processing

check.q: A pipeline upserts into a table by primary key and must be fast. Which design is most sensible?
opts: At least once delivery with keyed upserts
Full transactions across every stage
At most once with no retries
check.why: Keyed upserts make duplicates harmless, so at least once gives the right result without transaction latency or complexity.

work: For each pipeline, write down the cost of one duplicate and the cost of one second of delay.
Prefer keyed upserts before reaching for end-to-end transactions.

reels.title: Tills and the counter display

beats.say: Why does a busy shop open more tills, yet a cafe keeps popular sandwiches on the counter?

show.text: More tills. Food on the counter.
show.sub: Two tricks for the same problem: too many people, too slow

beats.say: A load balancer is the person at the door, pointing each shopper to a till. If a till breaks, they stop sending anyone there. That check is called a health check.
A cache is the counter display. Fetching from the kitchen is slow, so popular items sit close by and customers get them instantly.

chip.text: Near is fast, far is slow

beats.say: The catch is freshness. If the kitchen changes the recipe, the counter copy is now wrong. So you bin old items after a set time, or the moment the recipe changes. Fast, but sometimes out of date.

show.title: The cache trade
items: Throw items out after a set time
Or throw out the moment the source changes

check.q: What is the main price of keeping a cache in front of a database?
opts: Reads get slower
The cached copy can be out of date
The database needs more disk
check.why: A cache is a copy. It trades freshness for speed, so you must expire or delete entries when the source changes.

work: List the services you own that read the same data repeatedly and could use a cache.
For one of them, write down how stale the data is allowed to be.

reels.title: Redial wisely, and the ticket jar

beats.say: Your friend does not answer the phone. Do you redial fifty times in a row?

No. You wait a bit, try again, then wait longer. Add a little randomness, so everyone you know does not call back at the same second. That is a retry with backoff and jitter. And you give up after a while.
Now picture a club bouncer with a jar of tickets. Each guest costs one ticket. The jar refills slowly. Empty jar, and guests are told to come back later. That is a rate limit.
If a service tells you to come back later, listen. Slow down. Hammering it makes things worse for everyone.

check.q: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
opts: So clients do not all retry at the same instant
So retries run faster
So the server can skip health checks
check.why: Without jitter, many clients that failed together retry together, creating another spike. Randomness spreads them out.

work: Check whether your ingestion jobs retry with backoff, or retry instantly.
Make your API clients read the Retry-After header when they get a 429.

reels.title: Cache-aside in numbers

beats.say: A database read takes fifty milliseconds. A cache read takes one. So how do you make most reads feel instant?
Cache-aside. The app asks the cache first. A hit returns in one millisecond. On a miss, the app reads the database, then stores the answer in the cache for next time.
With a ninety percent hit rate, the average read drops from fifty milliseconds to about six.
Stale data is the price. So when a row changes, delete its key, often triggered by change data capture. Also set a time to live, say five minutes, as a safety net if a delete is missed.

show.title: Keeping it fresh
items: Change data capture can trigger the delete
Time to live of 5 minutes as a safety net

check.q: A row is updated in the database. What is the usual cache-aside response?
opts: Wait for the entry to expire on its own
Delete the cached key and keep a time to live as a backup
Copy the whole database into the cache
check.why: Deleting on write keeps data fresh. The time to live is only a safety net if a delete is missed.

work: Measure the real hit rate of one cache you run; below 80 percent, question its value.
Make sure every cache entry has a time to live.

reels.title: The token bucket

beats.say: How can an API allow a burst of traffic, yet still cap the average?
With a token bucket. Each client has a bucket holding, say, one hundred tokens. It refills at ten tokens a second. Every request spends one.
A quiet client can burst one hundred requests at once. After that, it is held to ten a second. Empty bucket means a 429 error, ideally with a Retry-After header.
With many servers, counters need a shared home like Redis, so limits are exact. Or each node counts alone with a looser limit, which is faster but approximate.

show.title: Limits across a cluster
items: Shared counter in Redis: exact, one extra hop
Set each node limit looser to allow for skew

check.q: A client with a full 100-token bucket and a 10 per second refill sends 100 requests in one second. What happens?
opts: All are allowed, then it is held to about 10 per second
Only 10 are allowed
All are rejected with 429
check.why: The bucket allows a burst up to its size. After it empties, the refill rate caps the average.

work: Pick separate burst and average limits for one API you own.
Return Retry-After with every 429 you send.

reels.title: Thundering herd and write-behind

beats.say: A hot key expires. Ten thousand requests arrive in the same second. What happens to your database?
Every request misses the cache, so every one hits the database together. This is a thundering herd, and it can knock the database over exactly when traffic is highest.
Fix one: a lock, so one request refills the key while the rest wait briefly. Fix two: refresh hot keys before they expire.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Lock: one request refills, others wait
Refresh hot keys before they expire
Add jitter to time to live values

beats.say: Write-behind has a different trap. Writes land in the cache and flush later, so if the cache dies first, those writes are gone. Use it only when losing a few seconds of data is acceptable.

check.q: Which technique prevents a thundering herd on an expired hot key?
opts: Write-behind
A lock so only one request refills the key
A longer database timeout
check.why: Letting one request rebuild the value while others wait stops thousands of identical database queries.

work: Find your hottest cache keys and check what happens when they expire.
Add random jitter to time to live values so keys do not expire together.

reels.title: Safe retries and idempotency keys

beats.say: A client times out on a payment request and retries. Did the customer just pay twice?

show.sub: Only if the write is not idempotent

beats.say: Retries are only safe for transient errors, like a timeout, never a bad request. Wait longer each time, with random jitter, so thousands of clients do not retry in lockstep.

show.title: Retry rules
items: Only transient errors, not bad requests

beats.say: They are only safe for idempotent operations, where doing it twice equals doing it once. For writes, the client sends an idempotency key with each request.

The server saves that key with the result in the same transaction. When the key comes again, it returns the saved result and does nothing new. The same rule protects replays and at-least-once delivery.

show.title: Server side
items: Store key and result in one transaction
Repeat key: return the stored result
Protects retries, replays and at-least-once delivery

check.q: Why must the server store the idempotency key and the result in the same transaction?
opts: It makes the key shorter
A crash between the two could cause a duplicate action or a lost record
It speeds up the database
check.why: If they were saved separately, a crash could leave the work done with no key, so a retry would repeat it.

work: Check which of your write endpoints are safe to retry.
Add an idempotency key to one ingestion endpoint and test a duplicate.

reels.title: Timeouts, breakers and bulkheads

beats.say: One slow dependency can take your whole service down. How?

show.text: One slow call. Whole service down.

beats.say: Calls without a timeout wait forever. Threads pile up, the pool empties, and now unrelated requests cannot get a thread either. So every remote call gets a timeout.

A circuit breaker watches failures. After too many, it opens and fails fast for a while, instead of piling more load on a struggling service. Then it lets a few test calls through to see if it recovered.
Bulkheads give each dependency its own pool of connections. If the recommendations service hangs, it drains only its own pool, and payments keep working.

check.q: What does an open circuit breaker do?
opts: Retries every call until it works
Fails calls quickly so the struggling dependency can recover
Doubles the thread pool
check.why: Failing fast stops more load piling onto a failing service and frees your own threads. It then probes with a few test calls.

work: Audit your remote calls for missing timeouts.
Give your slowest or flakiest dependency its own connection pool.

reels.title: Scale up, scale out, then shard

beats.say: Traffic is growing and the database is slow. Do you shard it tomorrow?

Almost never first. Fix queries and indexes. Add a cache. Add read replicas. Partition big tables. Scale the machine up. Only then shard, because sharding makes joins, transactions and operations much harder.
Scaling out needs stateless servers and work that can be split. Scaling up is simpler and often cheaper until it hits a ceiling.

show.title: Up versus out
items: Up: simple, often cheaper, has a ceiling
Out: needs work that can be partitioned

beats.say: For pipelines, the same thinking is data locality: move computation to the data. A Spark task runs where its blocks live, because shipping code is cheaper than shipping terabytes.

check.q: A database is slow and read heavy. Which step comes before sharding?
opts: Adding a cache and read replicas
Rewriting every table key
Splitting into many databases by user
check.why: Caches and replicas absorb reads cheaply. Sharding is the last resort because it complicates joins and transactions.

work: Write the scaling ladder for your busiest database and mark which rungs you have used.
Before proposing sharding in a design, state which cheaper steps you ruled out and why.

reels.title: All or nothing: what a transaction promises

beats.say: What happens if the power dies halfway through moving a hundred dollars between two bank accounts?

show.sub: Money out of A, not yet into B?

beats.say: A transaction is a bundle of steps treated as one. Either every step happens, or none do. That is atomicity. Without it, money could leave one account and never arrive in the other.

ACID has three more promises. Consistency means your own rules hold, like balances never going negative. Isolation means people working at the same time do not trip over each other. Durability means once the bank says done, it stays done, even after a crash.

show.title: The rest of ACID
items: Isolation: simultaneous work does not collide
Durability: committed means saved, even after a crash

check.q: A transfer removes money from account A but the system crashes before adding it to B. Which ACID property should undo the removal?
opts: Atomicity
Durability
Isolation
check.why: Atomicity means all steps of the transaction happen or none do, so the half-finished transfer is rolled back.

work: List the multi-step writes in your pipelines that must succeed together, and check each runs inside one transaction.
Ask which of your data stores give you real transactions and which only give single-row guarantees.

reels.title: Lost updates, isolation levels and snapshots

beats.say: Two jobs read a counter showing ten. Both add one. Both write eleven. Where did the other increment go?

That is a lost update. Each job worked from a stale read, and the second write overwrote the first. Fix it by letting the database do the math: update the counter, set n equals n plus one. Row locks or compare and set also work.

show.title: Atomic fix
show.text: UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1;
show.note: The read and write happen as one step

beats.say: Isolation levels decide which anomalies you tolerate. Read committed stops dirty reads, meaning you never see uncommitted data. Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a frozen view, so repeated reads match. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

show.title: Each level prevents more
items: Snapshot: stable view for the whole transaction
Serializable: as if one at a time

beats.say: Snapshots work through MVCC. The database keeps old row versions, so readers never block writers.

show.sub: Old versions kept, so readers do not block writers

check.q: Two jobs read n = 10, each adds one and writes back, and the result is 11. What is the best fix?
opts: Run the jobs more slowly
Use an atomic UPDATE that sets n = n + 1
Switch to dirty reads
check.why: An atomic update does the read and write in one step inside the database, so neither increment can be overwritten.

work: Search your code for read, modify, write patterns on counters or balances and replace them with atomic updates.
Check which isolation level your main database uses by default and write it down.

reels.title: Write skew: when snapshots are not enough

beats.say: Two engineers each check that someone else is on call, then both go off call. Nobody checked wrong. So who broke the rule?

That is write skew. Under snapshot isolation, each transaction sees a frozen view where the other engineer is still on call. They update different rows, so no conflict is detected. Together they leave zero people on call.

show.title: Why nothing stops it
items: Each read was valid in its own snapshot

beats.say: Only serializable isolation, or explicit locks on the rows you read, prevents it. Postgres serializable spots the dangerous pattern and aborts one transaction, so your app must retry. Note that Postgres repeatable read is snapshot isolation, and it is not enough here.

check.q: Under snapshot isolation, two transactions read the same set of rows, then each updates a different row, breaking a rule across the set. What is this?
opts: Dirty read
Lost update
Write skew
check.why: Write skew happens when writes to different rows together violate an invariant that each transaction checked separately. Snapshot isolation does not catch it.

work: Find rules in your system that span several rows, such as minimum staffing or stock limits.
For each, use serializable isolation or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the rows you check, and add retry logic.

reels.title: Deadlocks and how to avoid them

beats.say: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. Who gives up?
Writes take an exclusive row lock, held until commit. If one transaction locks row A then B, while another locks B then A, each waits forever. The database spots the cycle and aborts one victim.

show.title: Two phase locking
items: All locks are released only at commit

beats.say: Your app must catch that error and retry. Better, prevent it. Lock rows in a fixed order, such as order by id for update. Keep transactions short, so locks are held for milliseconds. Never hold one open while waiting on a user or an API call.

show.title: Fixed lock order
show.text: SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
show.note: Everyone locks in the same order, so no cycle

check.q: Which habit best prevents deadlocks between transactions that update the same set of rows?
opts: Lock the rows in a consistent order, such as by id
Use larger transactions
Lock rows in whatever order is convenient
check.why: A deadlock needs opposite lock orders. If every transaction locks in the same order, a waiting cycle cannot form.

work: Make sure your application retries when the database aborts a transaction as a deadlock victim.
Review code that updates multiple rows and sort the keys before locking.

reels.title: Why two merges on one Iceberg table collide

beats.say: Why did your second merge job on the same Iceberg table fail with a commit conflict?
A lakehouse table is a series of snapshots. Readers pick one snapshot and see a stable view, never blocked. Writers take no locks. They prepare new files, then try to commit a new snapshot.
That is optimistic concurrency. If another job committed first, your commit is rejected, and you retry against the new snapshot. If both touched the same files, the retry itself conflicts and fails.
So schedule merges on one table so they do not overlap, or split the work so jobs touch different files.

show.title: Avoid conflicts
items: Do not overlap merges on one table
Partition so jobs touch different files

check.q: Two concurrent MERGE jobs update the same files of a table. What most likely happens?
opts: Both succeed and rows are silently mixed
The first to commit wins and the other fails or retries with a conflict
The table locks readers until both finish
check.why: Table formats commit optimistically. The loser sees a newer snapshot, retries, and fails if the changes truly overlap. Readers are never blocked.

work: Check whether your orchestrator can run two writers on one table at the same time, and serialize them if so.
Partition merge workloads so concurrent jobs touch disjoint files.

reels.title: Choosing an isolation level on purpose

beats.say: Should you just run everything at serializable to be safe?

show.sub: Safe, but what does it cost?

beats.say: Serializable costs throughput or causes aborts, so retries become part of your design. Read committed is fast but allows lost updates. Most systems keep the default and fix the few risky paths with atomic updates or row locks.
Use serializable only where an invariant spans rows, like on-call rules or inventory limits. Across regions, Spanner gives serializable but pays in commit latency.
For lakehouses, optimistic commits suit batch writes. But a hot table with many small writers will thrash on retries. Funnel writes through a queue, or partition by writer.

check.q: A table receives thousands of tiny concurrent commits per minute and most fail on conflict. Best response?
opts: Retry harder with no delay
Batch writes through a queue or partition by writer
Move to read committed
check.why: Optimistic concurrency thrashes under heavy contention. Batching reduces commit count, and partitioning avoids overlap.

work: Document the isolation level each critical table or service needs, and why.
Reserve serializable for cross-row invariants, and measure abort rates before rolling it out widely.
Batch writes into hot lakehouse tables instead of committing per event.

reels.title: Keyset pagination and connection pools

beats.say: Why does page ten thousand of your API take seconds while page one is instant?

A large offset makes the database read and discard every skipped row. Page ten thousand at fifty per page throws away half a million rows. Keyset pagination says where id is greater than the last seen id, order by id, limit fifty. It jumps straight in using the index. The trade-off: no jumping to an arbitrary page number.

show.title: Keyset pagination
show.text: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

beats.say: Also put a connection pool in front. Each database connection costs memory and a process, so a few hundred is a ceiling. A pool shares them across requests instead of opening one per request.

check.q: Why is OFFSET 500000 slow on a large table?
opts: The database must read and discard 500000 rows first
It locks the whole table
It disables the index on id
check.why: Offset has no shortcut: rows are read in order and skipped. Keyset pagination uses the index to start right after the last seen key.

work: Replace deep OFFSET paging in your APIs with keyset pagination on an indexed, unique ordering column.
Size your connection pool to what the database can handle, and check that no service opens a connection per request.
